html:
The Germanic peoples were the tribes of northern Europe who spoke Germanic languages, between the Rhine, the Vistula, the Danube and southern Scandinavia. The map shows the label in 400 BCE, when they lived north of the Celtic world.

Their roots are usually traced to the Nordic Bronze Age and the Iron Age Jastorf culture of northern Germany. They lived in farming villages of long houses shared with their cattle, with no towns, and were led by chiefs and their war bands.

They entered Roman history with the Cimbrian War, when the Cimbri and Teutones invaded Gaul and Italy from 113 BCE until Marius destroyed them in 102 and 101 BCE. Caesar fought them on the Rhine. In 9 CE Arminius wiped out three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and Rome gave up trying to conquer the land east of the Rhine. Tacitus' Germania of 98 CE describes them, admiringly and not always accurately.

In the Migration Period of the 300s to 500s CE, Germanic peoples such as the Goths, Franks, Vandals and Saxons crossed the frontier and built the kingdoms that replaced the Western Roman Empire.
